title: OCD 18 — Test
src: White lesions of the oral cavity

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a reason an oral lesion appears white?
mcqs.explain: White lesions arise from thick epithelium, abnormal keratin, reduced blood supply or altered permeability — not melanin (which is brown).

mcqs.q: A bilateral grayish-white, filmy buccal lesion that DISAPPEARS when the mucosa is stretched is:
mcqs.explain: Leukoedema is a normal variant that fades on stretching; no treatment is required.

mcqs.q: Frictional hyperkeratosis is caused by:
mcqs.explain: Excess keratin forms in response to chronic friction; removing the cause resolves it.

mcqs.q: Leukoplakia is defined as a predominantly white lesion that:
opts: Cannot be characterised as any other definable lesion
mcqs.explain: Leukoplakia is a diagnosis of exclusion and is potentially malignant.

mcqs.q: Leukoplakia is best classified as a:
mcqs.explain: Some leukoplakias transform into cancer — it is a potentially malignant lesion.

mcqs.q: Which clinical type of leukoplakia carries the HIGHER malignant risk?
mcqs.explain: Non-homogeneous (speckled/nodular) leukoplakia has a higher risk than homogeneous types.

mcqs.q: Which oral sites show the HIGHEST malignant transformation of leukoplakia?
opts: Floor of mouth and lateral border of tongue
mcqs.explain: Floor of mouth and lateral/ventral tongue carry the highest transformation risk.

mcqs.q: Leukoplakia is definitively diagnosed by:
mcqs.explain: Biopsy (supported by cytology) is needed to assess dysplasia.

mcqs.q: Full-thickness epithelial dysplasia (without invasion) is termed:
mcqs.explain: Dysplasia involving the entire epithelial thickness = carcinoma in situ.

mcqs.q: Which is a histological feature of epithelial dysplasia?
mcqs.explain: Dysplasia shows drop-shaped rete ridges, loss of stratification, pleomorphism, hyperchromatism and abnormal mitoses.

mcqs.q: Oral submucous fibrosis is principally caused by:
mcqs.explain: Areca/betel nut chewing is the chief cause (with iron/folate deficiency, chillies and tobacco as cofactors).

mcqs.q: A hallmark clinical feature of OSMF is:
mcqs.explain: Fibrous bands cause blanched, stiff mucosa, loss of elasticity and progressive trismus.

mcqs.q: OSMF is regarded as a:
mcqs.explain: Untreated OSMF can progress to squamous cell carcinoma.

mcqs.q: Histology of OSMF characteristically shows:
opts: Dense fibrosis with reduced vascularity and hyalinisation
mcqs.explain: OSMF shows sub-epithelial fibrosis, decreased vascularity, epithelial atrophy/dysplasia and hyalinisation.

mcqs.q: The commonest organism causing oral candidiasis is:
mcqs.explain: Candida albicans is the usual cause; immunosuppression is the major predisposing factor.

mcqs.q: Pseudomembranous candidiasis (thrush) is distinguished clinically because the white plaque:
opts: Wipes off leaving a red base
mcqs.explain: The pseudomembrane of thrush wipes off, exposing an erythematous mucosa.

mcqs.q: Red, inflamed mucosa confined to the area beneath a denture indicates:
mcqs.explain: Denture stomatitis is a chronic erythematous candidiasis under a denture-bearing area.

mcqs.q: Candida is conveniently demonstrated in tissue using which stain?
mcqs.explain: PAS highlights fungal hyphae/yeasts; culture confirms the species.

mcqs.q: Oral lichen planus is thought to be mediated by:
mcqs.explain: Lichen planus is an immunologically mediated (T-cell cytotoxic) disease of unknown trigger.

mcqs.q: The cutaneous '6 P's' of lichen planus include all EXCEPT:
mcqs.explain: The 6 P's are pruritic, planar, purple, polygonal papules (reticular) — not pustular.

mcqs.q: The classic appearance of reticular oral lichen planus is:
mcqs.explain: Reticular lichen planus shows bilateral lace-like (Wickham's) white striae, usually on buccal mucosa.

mcqs.q: Which forms of oral lichen planus most warrant follow-up for malignant change?
mcqs.explain: The erosive and atrophic forms carry the greatest concern for malignant transformation.

mcqs.q: The serological hallmark of lupus erythematosus is:
mcqs.explain: ANA are the serological marker; histology resembles lichen planus and LE cells appear on smear.

mcqs.q: Which is one of the four main types of lupus erythematosus?
mcqs.explain: The four types are systemic, discoid, drug-induced and neonatal lupus erythematosus.

mcqs.q: Geographic tongue (benign migratory glossitis) is:
mcqs.explain: Geographic tongue is a harmless map-like condition that often improves on its own.

mcqs.q: Geographic tongue is frequently associated with:
mcqs.explain: It is linked to psoriasis, fissured tongue, and possibly stress/vitamin deficiency.

mcqs.q: Treatment of frictional hyperkeratosis is mainly:
mcqs.explain: Eliminating the source of friction (and habits) allows the keratosis to resolve, with follow-up.

mcqs.q: First-line conservative measures for leukoplakia include:
mcqs.explain: Remove the cause; retinoids and surgical excision (scalpel, cryo, electro, laser) are used as needed.

mcqs.q: Identify this mixed red-white, non-homogeneous lesion.
mcqs.explain: A mixed red-white (speckled) plaque is non-homogeneous leukoplakia — higher malignant risk.

mcqs.q: This patient can barely open the mouth after years of betel-nut chewing. The condition is:
mcqs.explain: Trismus from fibrous bands after areca-nut chewing is oral submucous fibrosis.

mcqs.q: Identify this white plaque that wiped off to leave a red base.
mcqs.explain: A wipe-off white pseudomembrane on a red base is thrush (pseudomembranous candidiasis).

mcqs.q: Identify the bilateral lacy white lesion shown.
mcqs.explain: Bilateral lace-like (Wickham's) striae are reticular oral lichen planus.

saqs.q: Give the definition of leukoplakia and state whether it is benign or potentially malignant.
saqs.a: A predominantly white lesion that cannot be characterised as any other definable lesion; it is potentially malignant.

saqs.q: List four histological features of epithelial dysplasia.
saqs.a: Drop-shaped rete ridges, loss of stratification, basal-cell hyperplasia, pleomorphism, hyperchromatism, increased/abnormal mitoses, increased N:C ratio.

saqs.q: Name the cause of oral submucous fibrosis and two clinical features.
saqs.a: Cause: areca (betel) nut chewing. Features: blanched/stiff mucosa with fibrous bands, and trismus.

saqs.q: Contrast pseudomembranous candidiasis and leukoplakia at the chairside.
saqs.a: Thrush (pseudomembranous candidiasis) wipes off leaving a red base; leukoplakia does not wipe off and needs biopsy.

saqs.q: A betel-nut chewer cannot open the mouth fully and has pale, leathery cheeks. Diagnosis and malignant potential?
saqs.a: Oral submucous fibrosis — a potentially malignant condition that can progress to squamous cell carcinoma.

saqs.q: List the four clinical forms of oral lichen planus and the form needing closest follow-up.
saqs.a: Reticular, plaque, atrophic/erythematous, erosive. Erosive (and atrophic) need follow-up for malignant change.
